Convolution to ConvNet
Convolution → ConvNetCMPT 361 · from one kernel to a whole network
Demo 1 · depth

When the image gets channels, the kernel gets depth

You know this picture for a grey image: a 3×3 kernel slides over a 2D grid and every stop produces one number. A colour image is three grids stacked. The kernel simply grows a matching third dimension — 3×3×3, one slab per channel — and each stop is now a sum of 27 products. The output is still one number per position: one kernel always makes one channel.

Timeline Kernel
image 12×12×1⊛ kernel 3×3×1→ output 10×10×1
out[y,x] = Σi,j K[i,j] · I[y+i, x+j]
Start here. Press Play. First the grey convolution you already know; then watch the image split into three channels and the kernel grow to match.
Demo 2 · width, then depth again

Many kernels make many channels — and the next kernels get deeper

One kernel gives one output map. Use five different 3×3×3 kernels on the same RGB image and you get five maps — stack them and you have a feature image with five channels. The next layer's kernels must therefore be 3×3×5. Seven of them give a seven-channel image, and the pattern repeats: number of kernels in = number of channels out.

Timeline Speed
input 12×12×3⊛ 5 kernels, each 3×3×3→ output 10×10×5
Round 1. Press Play. Each of the five kernels slides over the whole RGB image in turn; each pass produces one 10×10 map, and the five maps stack into a 10×10×5 feature image.
Demo 3 · the whole network

A small ConvNet, end to end, on CIFAR-10

Three convolution layers (16, 32 and 64 kernels), each followed by ReLU and 2×2 max-pooling, then one fully connected layer to 10 scores. It was trained on 20 000 CIFAR-10 images and gets – of unseen test images right. Pick an image, then click any box in the pipeline: feature maps show what each layer computes, the dashed boxes show the learned kernels, and the last box is the answer — a 10-number vector the network was taught to make one-hot.
